analysisMarkdown:
## Market Overview

Gold is trading at **$4,359 per ounce**, up **0.30% on the day** and **6.91% over the past 30 days**. That gain tells the story of a recovery: over the last month the metal has climbed from a low near **$3,982** back toward the range high around **$4,393**, and it now sits just below that ceiling.

The bigger backdrop matters. Gold set an all-time high above **$5,500** in late January 2026 before suffering its steepest quarterly decline in a decade during the spring. What we are watching now is the market repairing that damage. Prices have stabilised well above the panic lows and are grinding higher — constructive, but not yet a confirmed breakout.

## Key Drivers

**The dollar (tailwind).** The Federal Reserve's broad, trade-weighted dollar index stands at **119.06, down 2.07 points over 30 days**. A weaker dollar makes gold cheaper for buyers outside the US and is one of the two most important forces behind bullion. Right now it is clearly working in gold's favour.

**Real yields (mild headwind).** The 10-year real (inflation-adjusted) yield is **2.40%, up 0.09 percentage points** over the month, with the nominal 10-year Treasury at **4.65%** and the 10-year inflation breakeven flat at **2.25%**. Higher real yields normally weigh on gold because they raise the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset. The notable point is that gold is holding near record territory *despite* historically elevated real yields — a sign that other forces are dominating the traditional relationship.

**Central-bank demand (structural tailwind).** This is the force overriding real yields. Official-sector buying has been exceptionally strong: central banks purchased a **record ~289 tonnes in Q2 2026** according to the World Gold Council, following a robust first quarter. Surveys show a large share of central banks intend to keep adding to reserves over the coming year. These are price-insensitive, long-horizon buyers who do not sell on a single Fed meeting or headline — a durable floor under the market.

**Retail and physical demand.** Bar and coin demand has run near its highest levels on record through 2026, reinforcing the message that both official and private buyers have used the spring correction to accumulate rather than exit.

**Analyst positioning.** Forecasts skew bullish for the year ahead. Goldman Sachs has reiterated a **$5,400 year-end 2026** target, other major banks have published targets in the **$5,000–$6,300** range, and even more conservative houses see gold averaging in the low-$4,000s. Expectations remain constructive, though the wide spread underscores genuine uncertainty.

## Technical Picture

The chart is best described as a **consolidation between two well-defined levels**:

- **Support:** the 200-day moving average around **$4,340**, which price is currently trading just above. This is the line in the sand for the medium-term uptrend.
- **Resistance:** the 50-day moving average near **$4,730**, which has capped rallies.

With spot near **$4,359**, gold is squarely in the middle of this band — what analysts have called technical "no-man's land." Momentum has improved (a near-7% monthly gain), but the metal has not yet cleared the 50-day, so the recovery is not fully confirmed. A close above the **$4,390–$4,400** range high would open the door toward the 50-day; a slip below the 200-day would warn that the correction is resuming.

## Short-Term Outlook (1–4 weeks): HOLD

The setup is balanced. The **weaker dollar** and relentless official-sector buying argue for higher prices, but gold is bumping against the top of its recent range with the **50-day moving average overhead** and **real yields ticking up**. That combination favours patience over chasing. We prefer to **HOLD**, adding on pullbacks toward the 200-day rather than buying into resistance.

- **Turns bullish** on a decisive close above ~$4,400 and a reclaim of the 50-day (~$4,730).
- **Turns bearish** on a break back below the 200-day (~$4,340) heading toward the $3,982 low.

## Long-Term Outlook (3–12 months): BUY

Over a 3–12 month horizon the structural case is compelling. **Record central-bank accumulation**, a **softening dollar**, resilient physical demand, and bullish institutional targets all point in the same direction. The fact that gold is defending record-adjacent levels even with elevated real yields shows how strong the underlying bid is. We treat dips toward the 200-day and the low-$4,000s as **accumulation opportunities** and rate the long-term view a **BUY**, with medium confidence given the wide range of forecasts.

## Risks

- **Real-yield spike:** a sustained move in 10-year real yields well above 2.5% would sharpen gold's opportunity-cost headwind.
- **Dollar reversal:** if the broad dollar turns higher, an important tailwind flips to a headwind.
- **Demand fatigue:** any meaningful slowdown in central-bank or physical buying would remove the market's key structural support.
- **Liquidity stress:** in a broad market shock, investors sometimes sell gold to raise cash, which can trigger sharp, temporary drawdowns even in a bull market.

**Bottom line:** the trend and the fundamentals favour gold over the medium term, but with price pinned below resistance, near-term patience is warranted. Hold now; accumulate the dips.
